title: Vayishlach: the limp (Genesis 32:32–33)
hook: Jacob limps from the wrestling, and Jews still avoid eating the sinew of the thigh

segments.voice: Yesterday, a gift, a prayer and two camps. Your line was prepare three ways. Today, what happened that night.

An old injury can go quiet for months. A knee from a bike crash, a wrist that never quite healed right. Then one cold morning it aches, and the day it came from comes back with it. The night before meeting Esau, Jacob is alone by the river Jabbok, and a man wrestles with him until dawn. Jacob won't let go without a blessing, and he walks away with a new name, Israel. He also walks away with something else.
screen: `THE OLD ACHE ON A COLD MORNING.` → `WRESTLING UNTIL DAWN.` → `A NEW NAME, AND SOMETHING ELSE.`

segments.voice: During the struggle, the man touched the hollow of Jacob's thigh, and it was wrenched. Jacob names the place Peniel, face of God, because, he says, I have seen God face to face, and I'm still alive. Then the Torah gives us a picture. The sun rose on him as he passed Peniel, and he was limping on his thigh. Morning light, a new name, and a limp. He isn't the same man who crossed the river. Then the Torah does something unusual: it steps out of the story to speak to the future. Therefore, it says, the children of Israel don't eat the sinew of the thigh, on the hollow of the thigh, to this day, because he touched Jacob's thigh there. In Hebrew, that sinew is the gid hanasheh. Tradition identifies it with the sciatic nerve, which runs down the back of the leg. And the practice is real. Jewish law forbids eating it, and there's a whole chapter of the Mishnah about it. Removing it from the hindquarter of an animal is slow, skilled work, and in some places kosher butchers find it simpler not to use the hindquarters at all. So one night by a river still shapes what's on the table, generations of dinners later. Why remember the limp, and not only the victory? A medieval book on the commandments says it's a sign: Jacob struggled, was hurt, and wasn't defeated. His children would struggle too, and endure. The limp isn't a shame to hide. It's a memory the body keeps, on purpose, so the story doesn't get lost.
screen: `THE HOLLOW OF THE THIGH, WRENCHED.` · `PENIEL: FACE OF GOD.` · `THE SUN ROSE ON A LIMPING MAN.` · `GID HANASHEH, TO THIS DAY.` · then, large: `THE LIMP REMEMBERS.`

segments.voice: Find a scar, on your body or one that doesn't show: a loss, a failure, a hard year, and put your hand on it if you can. Remember the night it came from: you wrestled, you were hurt, and you're still here. Don't rush to fix the memory; let it be part of your story, the way the limp is part of Jacob's.
Gid hanasheh. The sinew of the thigh, which Jews don't eat, in memory of Jacob's limp after he wrestled until dawn.
Your line: the limp remembers. Jacob was hurt, and he was not defeated. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Kosher butchers remove the gid hanasheh, the sciatic nerve, from the hindquarter in a skilled process called nikkur, and in some places the hindquarters are simply not sold as kosher.

fork.setup: you've wrestled all night, won a blessing and a new name, and you're limping. you're telling your children the story. what do you leave in?
fork.reveal: the Torah keeps both, and even turns the limp into a lasting practice: the gid hanasheh isn't eaten, to this day.
